main.title: Super Mario Bros. 2
main.summary: Nintendo reworks Doki Doki Panic into a different Super Mario sequel for the NES. The Western Super Mario Bros. 2 follows a separate path from the difficult Japanese sequel.

cards.heading: A different sequel for Western audiences
cards.text: Super Mario Bros. 2 is Nintendo's 1988 NES platform game, adapted for international release from Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic. Nintendo of America had considered Japan's 1986 sequel too similar to the original and too difficult for its audience. The replacement gave Mario, Luigi, Princess Toadstool and Toad the roles of Doki Doki Panic's four protagonists, bringing their different abilities into the Mario series. It reached North America on 9 October 1988, followed by Europe and Australia on 28 April 1989.

cards.heading: Super Mario USA and the later remakes
cards.text: The game was a resounding success, becoming the fifth-best-selling game on the NES, and was critically well-received for its design aspects and for differentiating the Super Mario series. It was re-released  in Japan for the Family Computer on September 14, 1992, as Super Mario USA, and has been remade twice, first included in the Super Mario All-Stars collection, released on July 14, 1993, for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System, and as Super Mario Advance, released as a launch game for the Game Boy Advance on March 21, 2001. It is included as part of the Virtual Console and Nintendo Classics services.

main.title: Super Mario Bros. 3
main.subtitle: The Mushroom Kingdom Learns to Travel
main.summary: World maps, transformations and secret routes expand Mario’s platforming adventure.

cards.heading: World maps, flight and transformations
cards.text: Super Mario Bros. 3 expands Nintendo's platform series with world maps, alternate routes, stored items and new transformations. Raccoon Mario can fly, Frog Mario changes movement underwater, and Tanooki Mario can become a statue. Each kingdom arranges short levels around a different theme, while the map gives players choices about the route between them.

cards.heading: The Map Gives Shape to the Journey
cards.text: The world map shows how levels connect. Toad Houses, fortresses and moving encounters sit along the route, and some paths offer a choice about where to go next. Stored items can be saved for a difficult stage rather than used immediately. Individual courses remain separate, but their order and the supplies carried between them become part of planning the journey.

cards.heading: Flying Without Erasing the Level
cards.text: An early version of Raccoon Mario's flight lasted too long, Toshihiko Nakago recalled, letting players bypass much of the ground below. The team connected takeoff to a running phase and a power meter. Players need enough space to build speed before leaving the ground. Flight opens routes above the level while still depending on the terrain used to begin it.

cards.heading: Every Transformation Rewrites a Gesture
cards.text: Power-ups change Mario's movement and attacks. The Super Leaf provides a tail and flight; the Frog Suit alters control underwater; the Tanooki Suit adds a statue transformation; and the Hammer Suit changes his attack. Choosing a form can make a particular section easier or help reach a secret. Each transformation gives familiar terrain another use.

cards.heading: Eight Worlds, Eight Ways to Change Scale
cards.text: Eight kingdoms organise the levels around different settings. Giant Land enlarges objects, Water Land emphasises swimming, Sky Land builds upwards and Dark Land concentrates fortresses and dangers. These themes change the obstacles players expect as well as the appearance of the map. Remembering a world can help prepare for the kind of movement its courses demand.

cards.heading: The Inventory Brings the Future Into the Map
cards.text: Items earned in Toad Houses and minigames enter an inventory accessible from the map. A suit, Super Star or cloud can be reserved until a course gives it particular value. Players choose whether to spend a reward now or preserve it for an unknown obstacle. Supplies therefore carry decisions from one level into the next.

cards.heading: Secrets Turn Replays Into Knowledge
cards.text: Hidden whistles, invisible blocks, overhead areas and optional routes reward exploring beyond the direct path. Some discoveries let players bypass whole worlds. Once learned, those secrets can be used on another playthrough to organise a different journey. Replaying improves jumping precision and also lets remembered information change the route.

main.title: Mega Drive / Genesis
main.subtitle: One machine, more than one identity
main.summary: Sega's 16-bit console changed its name across regions, carrying a growing library from its Japanese launch into different markets and memories.

cards.heading: Inside Sega's 16-bit hardware
cards.text: The Sega Genesis, known as the Mega Drive outside North America, is a 16-bit fourth generation home video game console developed and sold by Sega. It was Sega's third console and the successor to the Master System. Designed by an R&D team supervised by Hideki Sato and Masami Ishikawa, the Genesis was adapted from Sega's System 16 arcade board, centered on a Motorola 68000 processor as the CPU, a Zilog Z80 as a sound controller, and a video system supporting hardware sprites, tiles, and scrolling. It plays a library of more than 800 games on ROM-based cartridges. Several add-ons were released, including a Power Base Converter to play Master System games. It was released in several different versions, some created by third parties. Sega created two network services to support the Genesis: Sega Meganet and Sega Channel.

cards.heading: Sonic replaces Altered Beast in the bundle
cards.text: In mid-1990, Sega president Hayao Nakayama hired Tom Kalinske to replace Michael Katz as CEO of Sega of America. Although Kalinske knew little about the video game market, he surrounded himself with industry-savvy advisors. A believer in the razor and blades model, he developed a four-point plan: cut the price of the console, create an American team to develop games targeted at the American market, expand the aggressive advertising campaigns, and replace the bundled game Altered Beast with a new game, Sonic the Hedgehog. The Japanese board of directors initially disapproved of the plan, but all four points were approved by Nakayama, who told Kalinske, "I hired you to make the decisions for Europe and the Americas, so go ahead and do it."

cards.heading: Sega CD, 32X and LaserActive
cards.text: Sega released Mega Drive add-ons including the Sega CD (Mega-CD outside North America), which plays games on compact disc and can display full-motion video; the 32X, a peripheral with 32-bit processing power that can display polygons for 3D gaming; and the LaserActive, developed by Pioneer, which runs Mega-LD  games on LaserDisc. None were successful, and the resulting hardware fragmentation created consumer confusion.

main.title: Snatcher
main.subtitle: The Fear of No Longer Recognizing Anyone
main.summary: On November 26, 1988, Konami releases Snatcher in Japan for the NEC PC-8801, the first version of a project that would reach MSX2 a few weeks later and later be reworked for other hardware.

cards.heading: The Fear of No Longer Recognizing Anyone
cards.text: Konami released Hideo Kojima's Snatcher for the NEC PC-8801 in Japan on November 26, 1988, followed by an MSX2 edition weeks later. The adventure follows an investigation in Neo Kobe, where artificial beings can replace humans. Text, detailed images, sound and brief action sequences give the cyberpunk story its pace. Later editions expanded the original with voice acting and a third act.

cards.heading: An Adventure That Thinks in Shots
cards.text: Menus let players examine details, question people and gather information. Choosing an action determines when another image, line or sound appears. Kojima's scripting controlled transitions, timing and effects, using the pauses between decisions to shape a scene. The original PC-8801 release already developed this approach without the voice acting of later editions.

cards.heading: Neo Kobe Is Reconstructed One Clue at a Time
cards.text: Locations, testimony, terminals and objects gradually establish Neo Kobe. The investigation moves between specialised police, domestic technology, nightclubs and people afraid of infiltration. Because Snatchers can replace humans, faces and behaviour become evidence as well as scenery. Players must connect observations to recognise when a familiar appearance hides something else.

cards.heading: Five Floppy Disks to Build a Future
cards.text: The first PC-8801 edition occupies five floppy disks. Its detailed images and FM audio share limited memory and storage with text, music and transitions. The original ends without the third act included in later versions. Comparing these editions reveals how the project expanded when different hardware and storage made a larger presentation possible.

main.title: Ninja Gaiden (NES video game)
main.summary: Ninja Gaiden, released in Japan as Ninja Ryūkenden and as Shadow Warriors in Europe, is a 1988 hack and slash platform game developed and published by Tecmo for the Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.heading: Ninja Gaiden (NES video game)
cards.text: Ninja Gaiden, released in Japan as Ninja Ryūkenden and as Shadow Warriors in Europe, is a 1988 hack and slash platform game developed and published by Tecmo for the Nintendo Entertainment System. Its development and release coincided with the beat 'em up arcade version of the same name. It was released in December 1988 in Japan, in March 1989 in North America, and in August 1991 in Europe. It has been ported to several other platforms, including the PC Engine, the Super NES, and mobile phones.

cards.heading: The design
cards.text: Set in a retro-futuristic version of 1988, the story follows a ninja named Ryu Hayabusa as he journeys to America to avenge his murdered father. There, he learns that a person named "the Jaquio" plans to take control of the world by unleashing an ancient demon through the power contained in two statues. Featuring side-scrolling platform gameplay similar to Castlevania, players control Ryu through six "Acts" that comprise 20 levels; they encounter enemies that must be dispatched with Ryu's katana and other secondary weapons.

cards.heading: Cinematics, challenge and lasting acclaim
cards.text: Ninja Gaiden has an elaborate story told through anime-like cinematic cutscenes. It received extensive coverage and won several awards from video gaming magazines, while criticism focused on its high difficulty, particularly in the later levels. Director Hideo Yoshizawa named Ninja Gaiden as his most commercially successful project, with over 1.8 million cartridges sold worldwide. The game continued to receive acclaim from print and online publications, being cited as one of the greatest video games of all time. It was novelized as part of the Worlds of Power game adaptations written by Seth Godin and Peter Lerangis. The game was followed by Ninja Gaiden II: The Dark Sword of Chaos (1990) and Ninja Gaiden III: The Ancient Ship of Doom (1991).

main.title: Final Fantasy II
main.summary: Final Fantasy II is a 1988 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer as the second installment of the Final Fantasy series.

cards.text: Final Fantasy II is a 1988 role-playing video game developed and published by Square for the Family Computer as the second installment of the Final Fantasy series. It was ported to and remade for WonderSwan Color, PlayStation, Game Boy Advance, PlayStation Portable, and mobile phones. Originally exclusive to Japan, later versions were released internationally, including the 2021 Final Fantasy Pixel Remaster version. The story follows the warrior Firion and his allies as they join a rebellion against the expanding Palamecian Empire. The gameplay is similar to the original game with an overworld and dungeon exploration, but its combat design is changed to a usage-based growth system where characters' statistics increase according to how they are used or acquired.

The game began development after the success of Final Fantasy, with the team using a new setting to make the game accessible to players. Returning staff included series creator Hironobu Sakaguchi as director, designer Akitoshi Kawazu, programmer Nasir Gebelli, artist Yoshitaka Amano, writer Kenji Terada, and composer Nobuo Uematsu. The team wanted to create a game that was different from the first Final Fantasy, including creating a narrative that drew inspiration from The Empire Strikes Back (1980), and redesigning the combat system. The stat growth system was created by Kawazu, and he later felt the team went too far in making the game different from the original.

Upon its release, Final Fantasy II received highly positive reviews in Japan; retrospective reviews have noted the game as having a stronger story than Final Fantasy, but have described it as among the most divisive entries in the series due to its progression system. As of 2003, the game sold over one million copies worldwide. Final Fantasy II saw the introduction of multiple series staples including chocobos and the recurring character Cid. Due to negative feedback, the next title Final Fantasy III (1990) reverted to the original combat system. Kawazu would continue using his system in the SaGa series, beginning with 1989's Makai Toushi SaGa (The Final Fantasy Legend) for the Game Boy.

cards.heading: Recognising the Apple II programmer
cards.text: Hiromichi Tanaka remembers Square's programmers and designers already knowing Nasir Gebelli's Apple II games before working with him. Masafumi Miyamoto brought Gebelli into contact with the company, and projects including WorldRunner and Rad Racer preceded Final Fantasy. In Tanaka's anniversary interview, the new role-playing game needed more than programming expertise. Tanaka supplied data design, experience tables and other systems work for Gebelli to implement. Their different experience met in the same game: an action programmer's technical ability alongside decisions about how a party should develop.

cards.heading: Keeping a project together abroad
cards.text: Tanaka recalled that Gebelli's visa expired before the Final Fantasy III master was ready. After Gebelli returned to the United States, colleagues followed him with equipment to continue the work. Finishing the game required keeping the small team in contact with the programmer who knew its code. People and hardware travelled together to preserve that working arrangement.

cards.heading: An airship carries a programmer's choice
cards.text: In a contemporary interview about Final Fantasy II, Hironobu Sakaguchi credited Gebelli with the first game's fast airship scrolling and a hidden overworld game. Other staff supplied gameplay systems for him to implement. The airship makes that division tangible: programming determines how smoothly the map passes below the party, alongside the design decision to let players travel across it.

cards.heading: A story also needs room in the program
cards.text: In that collection, Sakaguchi and writer Kenji Terada describe negotiating between story and game systems. Terada worked from an outline supplied by the team, trying to create something of his own within it. Sakaguchi then had to judge what the program and design could accommodate, leaving some ideas for another project. This exchange sits alongside Gebelli's technical work rather than replacing it. The game emerged through connected decisions about data, writing and implementation, with each contributor changing what the others could actually deliver.

main.title: Mega Man 2
main.subtitle: Every opponent leaves behind a possibility
main.summary: On December 24, 1988, Capcom released Rockman 2 in Japan, later known as Mega Man 2, for Famicom.

cards.heading: Every opponent leaves behind a possibility
cards.text: Capcom released Rockman 2 for the Famicom in Japan on December 24, 1988, later bringing it overseas as Mega Man 2. Eight selectable Robot Masters expand the first game's weapon-and-weakness system. Energy Tanks let players save recovery for a difficult moment, while passwords preserve progress between sessions. Distinctive stages and music give each opponent a setting of its own.

cards.heading: Eight Robot Masters turn order into strategy
cards.text: Players choose which of eight Robot Masters to challenge first. Defeating one awards a weapon that may be particularly useful against another. A later attempt at a difficult stage can therefore begin with different equipment. Learning the bosses' weaknesses helps organise a route, alongside the platforming skill needed to reach them.

cards.heading: The Energy Tank separates recovery from the moment it is found
cards.text: Energy Tanks store a full recovery until the player chooses to use it. A tank collected earlier can be held for a boss or spent to survive the current section. Supplies are limited, so using one now reduces the reserve for later. This addition gives players another way to prepare without changing the jumps and hazards they must cross.

cards.heading: The password turns a series of levels into a resumable campaign
cards.text: A grid of dots records progress without requiring save memory in the cartridge. Copying the password allows the player to resume after defeating particular Robot Masters. Boss victories can therefore carry across separate sessions. The practical task is keeping an accurate copy: a misplaced dot can prevent the recorded progress from being restored.

cards.heading: An apparently weak weapon can become the only answer
cards.text: A weapon's first appearance may not reveal every use. Capcom has highlighted Bubble Lead, which can seem weak but reveals certain traps and becomes important in the final section. Trajectory, cost and special properties matter alongside damage. Trying acquired weapons in different situations can reveal an answer to an obstacle much later in the game.

cards.heading: Graphical limits become a choice of form
cards.text: Designer Naoya Tomita recalled working within the early games' graphical limits. In discussing the Mecha Dragon battle, Capcom described platforms using a single colour arranged to suggest depth and shadow. Walkable surfaces and hazards still had to remain clear around a large boss. Carefully chosen contrasts made a constrained image readable during movement.

cards.heading: Music gives every level an identity before the boss
cards.text: Each Robot Master has a stage with a distinct rhythm, colour and musical theme. Takashi Tateishi composed the well-known music for the first section of Wily's castle. Limited Famicom sound channels had to accommodate these melodies alongside the effects of constant movement and shooting. Repeated attempts made the music closely associated with the route the player was learning.

main.title: Atari Lynx
main.subtitle: Turn the screen around
main.summary: A colour handheld could change its orientation to suit the player's hands and link with other machines for shared games.

cards.text: Atari's Lynx arrived in 1989 with a colour screen in a broad handheld case. Its controls and display could change orientation to suit the game or the player's hands. Compatible games could also connect several nearby machines, each with its own screen.

Atari's original manual explains a revealing feature: players could turn the machine around and flip its image, moving the directional pad from the left hand to the right. Games designed for a vertical screen could be held another way again. The arrangement treated orientation as a choice rather than a fixed assumption. Duplicated action buttons made that choice practical in the physical case.

A ComLynx cable links compatible games across separate handhelds. Each player keeps a personal screen while joining the same session. The original model runs from batteries or an adaptor and has a wider case than the later Lynx II. Colour, reversible orientation and linked play were central features of this first design.

main.title: DuckTales
main.subtitle: A fortune at the end of a pogo jump
main.summary: Capcom’s DuckTales brought Scrooge McDuck to the NES in 1989. His search for five lost treasures stretches from the Amazon to the Moon, with the player choosing a destination from the control room. The familiar Disney cast supplies the setting, but Scrooge’s cane gives the adventure its own physical language.

cards.heading: A fortune at the end of a pogo jump
cards.text: Capcom’s DuckTales brought Scrooge McDuck to the NES in 1989. His search for five lost treasures stretches from the Amazon to the Moon, with the player choosing a destination from the control room. The familiar Disney cast supplies the setting, but Scrooge’s cane gives the adventure its own physical language.

cards.heading: The cane, the treasure and the Moon
cards.text: The cane serves both as a striking tool and as a pogo stick: bouncing changes how Scrooge crosses dangerous ground, breaks obstacles and meets enemies. Diamonds, hidden passages and helpful characters encourage more than a straight run to the exit. Hiroshige Tonomura’s original music gives each destination a distinct identity; the NES Moon theme belongs to this 1989 game, rather than the later orchestral and electronic arrangements made for DuckTales: Remastered.

main.title: Golden Joystick Awards 1989
main.summary: The Golden Joystick Awards, with every category winner of the 1989/1990 edition.

cards.heading: The players' awards
cards.text: The Golden Joystick Awards celebrate games through a public vote, bringing players into the choice of each year's winners. The awards began in Britain with the 1983 season and later reached an international audience through online voting. Their changing categories trace the growth of games: home computers and consoles, handhelds, online play, independent studios, performance and music. Alongside the public vote, special honours recognise individual contributions to the industry. Each edition preserves its own category names, so the results also show what players and the awards organisers considered worth celebrating at the time.
